Vatican City :: Demographics :: Languages :: chunk_0030
Further information: [Languages of Vatican City](/wiki/Languages_of_Vatican_City "Languages of Vatican City")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Seal_of_Vatican_City.svg/250px-Seal_of_Vatican_City.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Seal_of_Vatican_City.svg)

The Seal of Vatican City. Note the use of the Italian language

Vatican City has no formally enacted [official language](/wiki/Official_language "Official language"), but, unlike the Holy See which most often uses [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin") for the authoritative version of its official documents, Vatican City uses only Italian in its legislation and official communications.[[141]](#cite_note-154) Italian is the everyday language used by most of those who work in the state. In the Swiss Guard, [Swiss German](/wiki/Swiss_German "Swiss German") is the language used for giving commands. Individual guards take their oath of loyalty in their own languages: German, French, Italian or [Romansh](/wiki/Romansh_language "Romansh language"). The official websites of the Holy See[[142]](#cite_note-155) and of Vatican City[[143]](#cite_note-156) are primarily in Italian, with versions of their pages in a large number of languages, to varying extents.

Corey Patterson :: Professional career :: Chicago Cubs :: chunk_0002
Patterson was selected by the [Chicago Cubs](/wiki/Chicago_Cubs "Chicago Cubs") as the third overall pick in the [1998 Major League Baseball draft](/wiki/1998_Major_League_Baseball_draft "1998 Major League Baseball draft"). He signed a five-year, $3.7 million contract that was the largest draft contract in history.[[4]](#cite_note-:6-4) He made his professional debut in 1999 with the [Lansing Lugnuts](/wiki/Lansing_Lugnuts "Lansing Lugnuts") of the Class-A [Midwest League](/wiki/Midwest_League "Midwest League") and won the league's [Prospect of the Year Award](/wiki/Midwest_League_Prospect_of_the_Year_Award "Midwest League Prospect of the Year Award") after leading the circuit in [slugging percentage](/wiki/Slugging_percentage "Slugging percentage") (.592), [extra base hits](/wiki/Extra_base_hit "Extra base hit") (72) and [triples](/wiki/Triple_(baseball) "Triple (baseball)") (17). He also batted .320 with 20 homers and 79 RBI, and was named to the league's all-star team both at mid-season and postseason. *[Baseball America](/wiki/Baseball_America "Baseball America")* named Patterson the league's top prospect.[[5]](#cite_note-5) After the 1999 season, he played in the [Arizona Fall League](/wiki/Arizona_Fall_League "Arizona Fall League") and was that league's youngest player. He batted .368 with 4 home runs, 24 RBI, and 8 stolen bases in 35 games, and was named to the league's all-star team.

In 2000, Patterson was promoted to the Double-A [West Tenn Diamond Jaxx](/wiki/West_Tenn_Diamond_Jaxx "West Tenn Diamond Jaxx") of the [Southern League](/wiki/Southern_League_(1964%E2%80%932020) "Southern League (1964–2020)"). He was named to the league's mid-season and postseason all-star team, and was named the league's top prospect by *Baseball America*. Patterson batted .268 with 22 home runs and 82 RBI, finishing second in the league in home runs.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)[[2]](#cite_note-:2-2)

fanoutqa_037664.x:
Great Smoky Mountains National Park :: Attractions and activities :: Sightseeing :: chunk_0023
The most frequented destination in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park is [Cades Cove](/wiki/Cades_Cove "Cades Cove"), a cleared valley that provides dramatic views of the surrounding mountains. Cades cove has numerous preserved historic buildings including log cabins, barns, and churches. Cades Cove is the single most frequented destination in the national park. An 11-mile (18 km) one-way loop road encircles Cades Cove. Self-guided automobile and bicycle tours offer the many sightseers a glimpse into the way of life of old-time southern [Appalachia](/wiki/Appalachia "Appalachia"). Other historical areas within the park include [Roaring Fork](/wiki/Roaring_Fork_(Great_Smoky_Mountains) "Roaring Fork (Great Smoky Mountains)"), [Cataloochee](/wiki/Cataloochee_(Great_Smoky_Mountains) "Cataloochee (Great Smoky Mountains)"), [Elkmont](/wiki/Elkmont,_Tennessee "Elkmont, Tennessee"), and the Mountain Farm Museum and Mingus Mill in [Oconaluftee](/wiki/Oconaluftee_(Great_Smoky_Mountains) "Oconaluftee (Great Smoky Mountains)").

The observation tower at [Kuwohi](/wiki/Kuwohi "Kuwohi"), the highest point in the park

At an elevation of 5,048 feet (1,539 m), it is the lowest gap in the crest of the mountains and is situated near the center of the park, on the Tennessee/North Carolina state line, halfway between Gatlinburg and Cherokee. Sergi Bruguera :: Career :: 1993–1994: Peak :: chunk_0002
Bruguera rose to even further prominence in 1993. During the [French Open](/wiki/1993_French_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_singles "1993 French Open – Men's singles"), Bruguera reached quarterfinals without dropping a set, including a rare triple bagel (6–0, 6–0, 6–0) in the second round against [Thierry Champion](/wiki/Thierry_Champion "Thierry Champion"); As of 2025 this remains the last time a player recorded a triple bagel in a singles match at a Grand Slam event.[[4]](#cite_note-4) He then defeated [Pete Sampras](/wiki/Pete_Sampras "Pete Sampras") in 4 sets and [Andrei Medvedev](/wiki/Andrei_Medvedev_(tennis) "Andrei Medvedev (tennis)") in straight sets in the semifinals, Bruguera reached his first [Grand Slam](/wiki/Grand_Slam_(tennis) "Grand Slam (tennis)") final at the French Open, where he faced two-time defending champion and then World No. 2 [Jim Courier](/wiki/Jim_Courier "Jim Courier"). Courier was overwhelmingly favoured to win his third title, but ultimately Bruguera won a gruelling five-set final that lasted 4 hours,[[5]](#cite_note-:bru1993fre-5) becoming the first Spaniard to win French Open since [Andrés Gimeno](/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_Gimeno "Andrés Gimeno") in 1972.[[5]](#cite_note-:bru1993fre-5) It was also the last time a man won a Grand Slam singles title with wins over both of the top two seeds until [Stanislas Wawrinka](/wiki/Stanislas_Wawrinka "Stanislas Wawrinka") won the Australian Open in 2014. He continued his top clay court player reputation by reaching finals at [Milan](/wiki/Milan "Milan") (his first final on Carpet), Barcelona, Madrid, and Palermo, while capturing an additional 4 titles at Monte Carlo (his 2nd ATP Masters 1000 title in singles), Gstaad, [Prague](/wiki/Prague_Open_(1987%E2%80%931999) "Prague Open (1987–1999)"), and Bordeaux (his 1st hard court title) besides Roland Garros. He finished the year ranked World No. 4.

**Pakistan**,[[f]](#cite_note-13) officially the **Islamic Republic of Pakistan**,[[g]](#cite_note-14) is a country in [South Asia](/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia"). It is the [fifth-most populous country](/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population "List of countries and dependencies by population"), with a population of over 241.5 million,[[d]](#cite_note-fn3-10) having the [second-largest Muslim population](/wiki/Islam_by_country#Countries "Islam by country") as of 2023. [Islamabad](/wiki/Islamabad "Islamabad") is the nation's capital, while [Karachi](/wiki/Karachi "Karachi") is [its largest city](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Pakistan_by_population "List of cities in Pakistan by population") and [financial centre](/wiki/Financial_centre "Financial centre"). Pakistan is the [33rd-largest country by area](/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area "List of countries and dependencies by area"). Bounded by the [Arabian Sea](/wiki/Arabian_Sea "Arabian Sea") on the south, the [Gulf of Oman](/wiki/Gulf_of_Oman "Gulf of Oman") on the southwest, and the [Sir Creek](/wiki/Sir_Creek "Sir Creek") on the southeast, it shares land borders with [India](/wiki/India "India") to the east; [Afghanistan](/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan") to the west; [Iran](/wiki/Iran "Iran") to the southwest; and [China](/wiki/China "China") to the northeast. It shares a maritime border with [Oman](/wiki/Oman "Oman") in the Gulf of Oman, and is separated from [Tajikistan](/wiki/Tajikistan "Tajikistan") in the northwest by Afghanistan's narrow [Wakhan Corridor](/wiki/Wakhan_Corridor "Wakhan Corridor").

The Kingdom of Denmark is a [unitary state](/wiki/Unitary_state "Unitary state") that comprises, in addition to metropolitan Denmark, two [autonomous territories](/wiki/Autonomous_administrative_division "Autonomous administrative division")[[13]](#cite_note-territory-20) in the [North Atlantic Ocean](/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"): the [Faroe Islands](/wiki/Faroe_Islands "Faroe Islands") and [Greenland](/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"). They have been integrated parts of the Danish Realm since the 18th century; however, due to their separate historical and cultural identities, these parts of the Realm have extensive political powers and have assumed [legislative](/wiki/Legislature "Legislature") and administrative responsibility in a substantial number of fields.[[113]](#cite_note-125) [Home rule](/wiki/Home_rule "Home rule") was granted to the Faroe Islands in 1948 and to Greenland in 1979, each having previously had the status of [counties](/wiki/Counties_of_Denmark "Counties of Denmark").[[114]](#cite_note-stm-126)

Wright 1899 kite: front and side views, with control sticks. Wing-warping is shown in lower view. (Wright brothers' drawing in Library of Congress.)

Despite Lilienthal's fate, the brothers favored his strategy: to practice gliding in order to master the art of control before attempting motor-driven flight. The death of British aeronaut [Percy Pilcher](/wiki/Percy_Pilcher "Percy Pilcher") in another hang gliding crash in October 1899 only reinforced their opinion that a reliable method of pilot control was the key to successful – and safe – flight. At the outset of their experiments they regarded control as the unsolved third part of "the flying problem". The other two parts – wings and engines – they believed were already sufficiently promising.[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouch2003166-37)

The Wright brothers' plan thus differed sharply from more experienced practitioners of the day, notably [Ader](/wiki/Cl%C3%A9ment_Ader "Clément Ader"), [Maxim](/wiki/Hiram_Maxim "Hiram Maxim"), and [Langley](/wiki/Samuel_Pierpont_Langley "Samuel Pierpont Langley"), who all built powerful engines, attached them to airframes equipped with untested control devices, and expected to take to the air with no previous flying experience. Although agreeing with Lilienthal's idea of practice, the Wrights saw that his method of balance and control by shifting his body weight was inadequate.[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobin200453-38) They were determined to find something better.

The timing of "fire season" in California is variable, depending on the amount of prior winter and spring precipitation, the frequency and severity of weather such as heat waves and wind events, and moisture content in vegetation. [Northern California](/wiki/Northern_California "Northern California") typically sees wildfire activity between late spring and early fall, peaking in the summer with hotter and drier conditions. Occasional cold frontal passages can bring wind and lightning. The timing of fire season in Southern California is similar, peaking between late spring and fall. The severity and duration of peak activity in either part of the state is modulated in part by weather events: downslope/offshore wind events can lead to critical fire weather, while onshore flow and Pacific weather systems can bring conditions that hamper wildfire growth.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:02-4)

The Bronx High School of Science was founded in 1938 as a specialized science and math high school for boys, by resolution of the [New York City Panel for Educational Policy](/wiki/New_York_City_Panel_for_Educational_Policy "New York City Panel for Educational Policy"), with [Dr. Morris Meister](/wiki/Morris_Meister "Morris Meister") as the first principal of the school. They were given use of an antiquated Gothic-gargoyled edifice located at Creston Avenue and 184th Street, in the [Fordham Road](/wiki/Fordham_Road "Fordham Road")-[Grand Concourse](/wiki/Grand_Concourse_(Bronx) "Grand Concourse (Bronx)") area of the Bronx. The building, built in 1918 for Evander Childs High School, had been successively occupied by [Walton High School](/wiki/Walton_High_School_(New_York_City) "Walton High School (New York City)") (1930) and by an annex of [DeWitt Clinton High School](/wiki/DeWitt_Clinton_High_School "DeWitt Clinton High School") (1935). The initial faculty were composed in part by a contingent from [Stuyvesant High School](/wiki/Stuyvesant_High_School "Stuyvesant High School").[[7]](#cite_note-stuyfac-7)

The Devils have been known as a defense-first team since head coach Jacques Lemaire's first tenure,[[208]](#cite_note-209) although the Devils have twice led the Eastern Conference in goals scored, once leading the NHL in goals scored (295 goals for in 2000–01).[[209]](#cite_note-210)[[210]](#cite_note-211) Lemaire gave the Devils their defensive mantra when he implemented a system commonly called the "[neutral zone trap](/wiki/Neutral_zone_trap "Neutral zone trap")".[[211]](#cite_note-212) This system is designed to force teams to turn over the puck in the neutral zone leading to a counterattack.[[212]](#cite_note-213) This style of play led the team to be chastised by the media and hockey purists for "making the NHL boring".[[213]](#cite_note-214) Nevertheless, the Devils were successful using this style of play, and Devils head coach Larry Robinson asserted that the Montreal Canadiens teams he played on in the 1970s (who also won the Cup many times) used a form of the trap, though it did not have a name.[[214]](#cite_note-215)

Under head coach [Brent Sutter](/wiki/Brent_Sutter "Brent Sutter"), the team adopted less of a trap and more of a transitional, aggressive forechecking style of play which also emphasized puck possession and instilled the cycle to start the 2007–08 season.[[215]](#cite_note-pressure-216) This led to many high scoring games early in the season for New Jersey. [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Coast_Redwood_fallen_branch_bark_tunnels.jpg/250px-Coast_Redwood_fallen_branch_bark_tunnels.jpg)](/wiki/File:Coast_Redwood_fallen_branch_bark_tunnels.jpg)

A recently fallen canopy branch reveals thin bark and tunnels made by bark beetle larvae.

Coast redwoods are resistant to insect attack, fungal infection, and rot. These properties are conferred by concentrations of [terpenoids](/wiki/Terpenoid "Terpenoid") and [tannic acid](/wiki/Tannic_acid "Tannic acid") in redwood leaves, roots, bark, and wood.[[58]](#cite_note-:03-58) Despite these chemical defenses, redwoods are still subject to insect infestations; none, however, are capable of killing a healthy tree. Bark is so thick on the bole that bark beetles cannot enter there. However, the canopy branches have thin bark (see photo at right) that native bark beetles are able to bore into for egg-laying and larval growth via tunnels.[[58]](#cite_note-:03-58)

Redwoods also face herbivory from mammals: [black bears](/wiki/American_black_bear "American black bear") are reported to consume the inner bark of small redwoods, and [black-tailed deer](/wiki/Black-tailed_deer "Black-tailed deer") are known to eat redwood sprouts.[[58]](#cite_note-:03-58)

The oldest known coast redwood is about 2,200 years old;[[9]](#cite_note-Gymnosperm-9) many others in the wild exceed 600 years. The numerous claims of older redwoods are incorrect.[[9]](#cite_note-Gymnosperm-9) Because of their seemingly timeless lifespans, coast redwoods were deemed the "everlasting redwood" at the turn of the century; in [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin"), *sempervirens* means "ever green" or "everlasting". Redwoods must endure various environmental disturbances to attain such great ages.
